title: An Existential Crisis in Higher Education
author: Patrick Dempsey
summary: Patrick Dempsey revisits the argument of his 2021 book on higher education, written before ChatGPT, that universities face an existential crisis because information is now ubiquitous and free. He argues that the usual fallback, critical thinking, is undermined by the lack of any agreed definition, so institutions are failing to deliver on it. His proposed answer is transformation, defined as openness to otherness, which he builds on the Community of Inquiry framework, transformative learning theory and complexity theory. Practically, he recommends fractal design repeated across program, course and assessment levels, learning objectives rewritten as the prompt for the task, clear instructions instead of rubrics that hide expectations, and instructional statements rather than questions. The piece closes by arguing that higher education's value lies in helping people become, not in transmitting content.
points: Dempsey argues that information ubiquity makes access to content an unsustainable basis for higher education's value.
He says critical thinking cannot carry the value proposition because the literature offers nineteen different definitions and institutions struggle to teach it.
He proposes transformation, an openness to otherness, as the aim, grounded in the Community of Inquiry, transformative learning and complexity theory.
He recommends fractal course design so the same structure repeats at every level and learners grasp expectations intuitively.
He would turn learning objectives into the learning task itself and replace rubric-hidden expectations with clear instructions.
quotes: Higher education today faces a significant existential crisis. The traditional model, which often relied on providing access to information, is no longer sustainable because information is now utterly ubiquitous and readily available for free on the internet.

However, despite this consensus, no one seems to be able to define what critical thinking actually is. The literature contains nineteen different definitions, ranging from internal evaluations to outward confidence, from mere open-mindedness to advanced information processing systems.

Transformation is understood less about being and more about becoming. It is not about adopting a specific ideology or worldview because others are wrong. Instead, it is a way of thinking that authentically makes room for the other.
This bias towards knowing certainly, rather than tentatively or not knowing at all, prevents genuine discourse and makes relationships impossible when individuals reject other possibilities a priori.

Teaching presence consists of course design, facilitation, and direction. It is shown to be of greatest value to students and critical in establishing the other presences. While the teacher holds significant responsibility, facilitation and direction are meant to be shared by the community. Teaching presence creates the space and opportunities for interaction of self and other.

Applying fractal forms creates robust, predictable environments that, through repeated exposure to and interaction with common forms, can lead to unexpected, transformative outcomes, much like grains of sand changing the form in an hourglass. This consistency provides valuable feedforward for learners.
This transforms the objective from a thin description to a thick experience that propels engagement and goes beyond mere apprehension.
